abstract: Interactive agents repeatedly choose among a finite set of actions, labels, or ordinal outcomes. Generating a free-form response for each choice adds latency and complicates the interface between a model and its environment. We present Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models that return structured choices and candidate probabilities from text and optional images. Our autoregressive masked language modeling objective places one decision placeholder per field in a complete assistant JSON skeleton. Ground-truth symbols appear only in supervision, while all fields are evaluated in a single causal forward pass using the backbone’s native language-model head. The 4B model achieves a 90.02% unweighted average accuracy across seven evaluation suites, compared with 88.74% for Jev v1.13.0. For a fixed 289-token request with three fields on one RTX 4090, mean latency is 44.16 ms for the 4B model and approximately 33–34 ms for the smaller models. On a separate 96-case known-distribution pilot, temperature scaling reduces expected multiclass Brier from 0.628 to 0.550 and expected calibration error from 0.213 to 0.089. A confidence-based handoff study on 111 public Jevbench-Hard items improves accuracy from 82/111 (73.87%) to 97/111 (87.39%) by routing 42 items to Atria-Dawn-Preview. We also describe qualitative game, visual interface, and browser demonstrations. These results support compact decision models as a practical component of larger agent systems.

sections.body: The paper argues that many agent decisions are closed-set choices that do not need free-form generation. It proposes Intern-Decision, a family of 0.8B, 2B, and 4B multimodal decision models built on Qwen3.5 backbones. Each request returns structured choices and candidate probabilities from one forward pass, with the vision tower and projector kept frozen. Temperature scaling is applied post hoc on a separate calibration split. Evaluation covers decision accuracy, latency, and probability quality, plus a confidence-based handoff to a larger model. The stated contributions are the model formulation, a unified framework, and the handoff study.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Intern-Decision proposes scoring finite agent choices in one causal pass, rather than free-form generation, for compact multimodal decision models.

sections.body: The section compares Intern-Decision with Jev, JevK5, Kev, SemIf-OpenJev, and Laya. These systems differ in their adaptation and scoring methods, including LoRA adapters, a learned pointer head, and encoder-based single-pass scoring. The paper states that Intern-Decision focuses on multimodal structured decisions. It also relates the method to masked-prediction work such as BERT, GPT-3, PET, and LM-BFF. Its native language-model head scores all requested fields without iterative refinement or answer feedback. For calibration, the paper cites temperature scaling and Brier scoring, and it reports one escalation point rather than an optimized routing policy.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Existing open decision models differ in how they score options, and Intern-Decision adds visual inputs to structured decisions.

sections.body: Each request has a state, optional images, and typed questions with ordered candidate sets. The model places one reserved decision token per field in an assistant output skeleton. Training applies full-vocabulary cross-entropy only at the shifted decision positions, using hard labels; skeleton punctuation and state tokens serve as context, not targets. Gold answers never enter the input, and earlier placeholders do not receive gold or predicted answers. At inference, logits for legal candidates are normalized with a temperature T, and the argmax gives the label. The paper notes that input cost still grows with state length, image tokens, and schema size, and that schema-conforming output does not guarantee semantic correctness.
sections.heading: Autoregressive Masked Decision Modeling
sections.headline: Each decision field gets one placeholder in an assistant output skeleton, and all fields are scored from one causal forward pass.

sections.body: The decision corpus combines synthetic textual decisions generated by deepseek-v4.1-flash, public task distributions, and synthetic visual and interactive tasks. The released checkpoints share 17,880 training samples and 23,500 decisions, including 5,500 image-bearing samples. The calibration test set is evaluation-only. It covers 24 mechanism families in six categories, with two settings per family and two option orders, giving 96 cases and 48 paired settings. Exact references are computed with rational arithmetic and kept out of model inputs. An exact-content check found no overlap with temperature-fitting records, but the paper states this does not rule out semantic overlap with every training source.
sections.heading: Data Construction
sections.headline: Training uses 17,880 samples and 23,500 decisions, while the 96-case calibration pilot is excluded from training and temperature fitting.

sections.body: Accuracy is the unweighted mean over seven suites: 90.02% for the 4B model and 88.74% for Jev. The 4B model scores 82/111 (73.87%) on Jevbench-Hard and 1,611/2,000 (80.55%) on Typed Decision. On the 111 Hard items, temperature scaling with T = 1.992418 reduces calibration error from 0.132613 to 0.065267 without changing the 82 correct decisions. Mean latency is 44.16 ms for a 289-token, three-field request on one RTX 4090, against 109.70 ms for Jev. The paper notes that public Jevbench informed development and is a diagnostic rather than held-out evidence, and that matched-data ablations are absent.
sections.heading: Evaluation Results
sections.headline: Intern-Decision-4B averages 90.02% unweighted across seven suites, above Jev at 88.74%, with 44.16 ms mean latency on a fixed request.

sections.body: The section describes a closed-loop interface in which the caller defines the action space and decides when to request another decision. The demonstrations are selected qualitative trajectories, not controlled benchmarks. Five game demonstrations cover Snake, fruit catching, Mario, and two Doom tasks. Four CAPTCHA-style pointer tasks are shown as successful runs without human correction. Three browser traces on public websites reach the requested evidence in 6, 6, and 4 local decisions, with server-reported median inference times of 101.6, 109.8, and 95.3 ms. The authors state that episode counts, seeds, returns, comparison policies, and browser benchmark results are needed for quantitative claims.
sections.heading: Multimodal Interaction and Model Collaboration
sections.headline: Qualitative demonstrations show Intern-Decision choosing game moves, mouse actions, and browser actions inside closed control loops, without benchmark scores.

sections.body: The conclusion describes Intern-Decision as a family that makes finite multimodal choices in one causal forward pass and exposes candidate probabilities through a typed interface. It reports that the 4B model has the highest seven-suite average in the presented comparison, with a 44.16 ms mean for a fixed short request on one RTX 4090. The calibration and handoff studies are presented as ways to support uncertainty analysis and selective use of a larger model. The authors state that generalization to arbitrarily large schemas and complex environments remains an open problem.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Intern-Decision is presented as a compact local decision component, with generalization to arbitrarily large schemas left unresolved.

sections.body: The appendix pins the public documentation to a Git revision and lists four evaluation stages, including requiring 96/96 valid pilot outputs. Table 8 gives full-precision temperature presets for each checkpoint, which the authors say are not freely transferable constants. Table 9 records shared training settings: two epochs, 156 optimizer updates, a global batch of 16 packed sequences at 8,192 tokens, BF16 precision on 4 GPUs, and the vision tower and projector frozen. Table 10 breaks the mixture into synthetic text, public tasks, and synthetic visual data. Appendix C lists the pilot families and worked cases, including a fair die with impossible faces and a socks-after-removal problem.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists release and reproduction steps, training settings, data examples, and worked calibration cases.
